title: ‘The Pacific is not for sale’: outcry after US holds first deep sea mining lease sale near American Samoa
text:
The US has carried out its first ever deep-sea mining lease sales off the coast of American Samoa, despite an adverse court ruling earlier this week and mounting local opposition.
The sales took place on Thursday in a live-streamed auction of 12.7m hectares (31.5m acres) of seabed off the US territory’s coast marked for mineral exploration. Two areas of the Pacific archipelago were sold for $3m each to Wetstone US Ventures, the only bidder, according to a spokesperson for the Marine Minerals Administration (MMA).
The buyers gain permission to conduct preliminary activities such as carry out bathymetric and geophysical mapping, among other data. The golf ball-sized metallic nodules that miners are searching for are touted as a source of rare earths and minerals needed for technologies, such as electric vehicles, renewable energy and defence systems.
“This is the first time the United States has held an offshore critical minerals lease sale in the Pacific and a historic step for America’s energy and mineral security,” said interior secretary Doug Burgum in a statement.
In his opening remarks at the California auction, Mike Olsen, director of the MMA, said the federal action today aligns with the Trump administration’s agenda “to advance the responsible development of America’s offshore critical mineral resources.”
“As we look to America’s next 250 years, we want future generations to inherit a nation that can build and innovate here at home, on the lands and in the waters that we’ve stewarded,” Olsen said.
However, the move comes despite a federal judge this week in Hawaii voiding the environmental clearance it had been given to proceed, ruling that the Endangered Species Act (ESA) had been violated. Judge Jill Otake wrote: “NMFS [National Marine Fisheries Service] failed to even attempt to consider the potential effects on ESA-listed species.”
Earthjustice, which filed the petition, said the ruling made Thursday’s auction unlawful. “We will use the full extent of the law to vigorously push for the leases to be voided,” Earthjustice attorney Chris Eaton said in a statement.
Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka, founder of Finafinau, an American Samoan youth and environment nonprofit, said: “More than 76,000 public comments, repeated calls for meaningful consultation, and now a federal court ruling that the government violated the Endangered Species Act. Yet here we are, watching our ocean being auctioned to the highest bidder.”
On the eve of the auction, Finafinau filed a fresh petition seeking an injunction with the district court of Hawaii in an unsuccessful last-minute bid to stop the lease sale. The lawsuit slammed the Trump administration for barrelling toward the sale “without sufficient information to comprehensively evaluate the impacts of issuing the first-ever commercial deep-sea mining leases”.
Taryn Kiekow Heimer, director of Ocean Energy at the non-profit Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC), warned that the American Samoa sale would now become the template for subsequent applications from mining companies.
“These leases last at least 20 years. The Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands and Guam are next in line,” Heimer said. “If this goes through, the administration will have shown it can open the deep sea over the objections of the people who live closest to it.”
A second lease sale involving 27.9m hectares (69m acres) of seabed between the Northern Mariana Islands and Guam is tentatively scheduled for 16 December. It is locked in a similar lawsuit that is pending in the federal court of Hawaii.
Guam Senator William Parkinson called on the US government to cancel the auction. “You don’t get to sell off our ocean first and ask whether it’s legal later. Washington needs to understand that the Pacific is not for sale,” he told the Guardian.
He said this week’s federal court decision “exposes the arrogance and recklessness of an administration that treats our ocean as a corporate commodity and Pacific Islanders as expendable.”
American Samoa governor, Pulaali’i Nikolao Pula, has previously said the deep sea mining auctions could “unlock scientiﬁc knowledge” and “create economic opportunities” for the territory.
John Wasko, an advocate of deep-sea mining, said the emerging industry, which is touted as supporting the electric vehicle sector, was the answer to climate change.
“Everybody wants unlimited renewable energy. Nobody wants to admit their part in planet Earth’s atmospheric destruction,” said Wasko, executive director of American Samoa Development Council, a non-profit group that endorses deep-sea mining in American Samoa.
The legal battle continues. In this week’s lawsuit, Finafinau asked the court to nullify the lease sale. “Despite venturing into largely uncharted territory, MMA recklessly accelerated environmental review,” its court filing states. “With this lease sale, the federal government has rushed to open the ocean floor to commercial mining for the first time, despite its limited understanding of the significant environmental consequences.”
